Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
245 PM EDT Tue Sep 22 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 245 PM EDT Tuesday...

Frost Advisories have been issued for the St. Lawrence Valley and 
eastern Clinton County in New York, as well as for Franklin, 
Lamoille, Chittenden, Washington, Orange, eastern Rutland, eastern 
Addison, and western Windsor Counties in Vermont from 2 AM to 9 AM

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 245 PM EDT Tuesday...

1. Seasonably cool and dry weather will continue through late 
week, with patchy frost tonight, and likely Wednesday night.

2. Still a large spread in potential outcomes associated with coastal 
system and if any rain/wind impacts our forecast area this weekend. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 245 PM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: High pressure is settling in across the region with 
clearing skies. The center of the high is actually to our north in 
southern Quebec, but we will still enjoy the clear and calm weather 
that is associated with it. Fair weather terrain cumulus will 
dissipate this evening with a few high clouds remaining across 
southern Vermont associated with a stationary boundary well south of 
the region in the Mid-Atlantic. Patchy fog and frost are expected 
tonight as clearing skies set up for good radiational cooling. 
Temperatures will dip below 40 degrees for majority of the area, 
outside of the wider valleys of southern Vermont. Widespread near 
freezing temperatures will be possible across the Northeast Kingdom, 
central Vermont, and the Adirondacks. Pocket mid to upper 20s will 
be likely in isolated portions of the northern Adirondacks. Frost 
Advisories have been issued for the St. Lawrence Valley and eastern 
Clinton County in New York, as well as for Franklin, Lamoille, 
Chittenden, Washington, Orange, eastern Rutland, eastern Addison, 
and western Windsor Counties in Vermont from 2 AM to 9 AM Wednesday. 
Frost will be less likely in areas near Lake Champlain, due to the 
surrounding warmer water temperatures helping to moderate the 
surrounding air. It should be noted that, as of 9/21, these products 
will no longer be issued for the Adirondacks and Northeast Kingdom, 
as median date of the first autumn freeze has passed. Thus, the 
growing season is considered ended in these areas.

Through the mid to late week, temperatures will slowly creep up a 
degree or two each day towards Thursday, with highs in the mid to 
upper 60s, as the high drifts to the east. Portions of the eastern 
Greens may see below normal temperatures continue Wednesday with a 
cold air damming setup. Frost potential will continue Wednesday 
night, though radiational cooling will be a touch weaker resulting 
in less areal coverage of any potential Frost Advisories. Fog 
chances will also see less coverage Wednesday night, though patchy 
fog in the climatologically favored valleys of eastern Vermont and 
the Adirondacks will still be possible. Clouds begin to build 
Thursday into Friday as a nor'easter off the southern New England 
Coast meanders. There is still a large degree of uncertainty with 
regards to the evolution of the system, as it pertains to cloud 
cover and precipitation chances. Currently it looks like Friday 
should remain dry for now with PoPs below 30%. Regardless, a 
tightening pressure gradient will develop across our area resulting 
in some breezy to channeled winds potentially Friday afternoon.

KEY MESSAGE 2: The long term forecast challenge is evolution and 
movement of deeply closed off sfc to 250mb cyclonic circulation and 
potential impacts to our cwa. Latest guidance continues to indicate 
a large spread in potential solutions between individual 
deterministic models and associated ensemble members, especially 
with regards to sfc low pres track and placement of precip. The 12z 
trends in guidance shows embedded short wave being captured in the 
cyclonic circulation, which helps to retro-grade sfc low pres 
westward toward the Mid-Atlantic/SNE coast by Sunday. The 12z 
ECMWF/ICON are most aggressive with advecting deep layer moisture 
back into parts of our cwa, while GFS/CMC shows better potential 
over central/eastern VT. The challenge will be a very sharp nw-se 
moisture gradient btwn coastal system and strong/dry high pres 
anchored over southern Canada. Could see band of moisture rotate 
around cyclonic circulation toward VT on Sat/Sunday and fall apart 
when they encounter deeper dry layer over our region. Latest WPC pop 
grids have cutback on precip chcs by 15% to 30%, which seems a 
little unreasonable given current trends. Feel these should be 
increases based on latest data, with highest probability of 
measurable precip acrs central/eastern and southern VT on Sat into 
Sun. 

Did note as the gradient increases between coastal low pres and 
sfc high pres, progged 925mb to 850mb winds increase at 30 to 45 
knots, which wl support a few gusts in the 20 to 35 mph range, 
especially higher trrn and aligned north to south valleys. Temps 
mostly in the 60s on Saturday/Sunday, and warm into the upper 60s to 
lower 70s by early next week. Lows in the mid 30s to mid/upper 40s, 
but could be warmer with more clouds/precip this upcoming weekend.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TUESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Through 18Z Wednesday...Aviation focus will be on timing and
coverage of fog tonight at our TAF sites. VFR conditions prevail
at all sites thru 06z with north/northeast winds 4 to 8 knots.
Winds become light tonight with clear skies, allowing for
favorable conditions for fog development. Highest probability
(60-70%) of fog/LIFR will be at SLK/MPV between 08-12z with
chance (30-40%) at EFK, and less than 20% at RUT/MSS/PBG and
BTV. Similar to last night, feel fog will be in the vicinity at
BTV and may impact the north end of the runway toward sunrise 
off the Winooski River. Otherwise, any fog/low clouds should 
lift by 13-14Z on Weds with VFR conditions prevailing. 

Outlook...

Wednesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Thursday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Thursday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.

Friday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
